children.text: Model Greenland as a rectangular island of width \(2L\), length \(5L\), with a flat bed at sea level. Ice height H(x) is independent of y, symmetric about the divide x=0, and vanishes at x=±L. Use \(\rho_i=917\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\rho_w=998\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(g=9.82\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), basal friction stress \(S_b=100\,\mathrm{kPa}\). Neglect atmospheric pressure. The integral \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u}\,du=2/3\) may be used. In the dynamical model, incompressible ice flows in the xz plane. Central snowfall adds ice thickness c per year, balanced by melting at the coasts. Near the divide take H≈Hm constant, vx independent of z, vz independent of x and vz=0 at the bed. The historical data and idealizations below are those of the 2013 problem.

Find H(x) and the maximum height Hm. Show the scaling with L.
The island area is A=10L². Find γ in \(V_{ice}\propto A^\gamma\), and derive the volume coefficient.
Use mass conservation in the central region to find vx(x).
A particle starts at \((x_i,H_m)\). Find its path z(x) in the central approximation.
Find the age τ(z) of ice at height z above ground at x=0.

A 3060 m core has the end of the ice age at depth 1492 m, 11,700 years ago. The ice age began 120,000 years ago at depth 3040 m. Assume Hm=3060 m throughout and constant rates c_ig and c_ia in each period. Find both in m/year.

Use Greenland area \(A_G=1.71\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), ocean area \(A_O=3.61\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) and the height profile to find the mean rise after all ice melts.

With a global ocean, no rotation, \(M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(R_E=6.38\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), find the sea-level difference between Copenhagen and the point antipodal to Greenland. Work to first order in sea height.

statement.text:
The Greenlandic Ice Sheet
Model Greenland as a rectangular island of width \(2L\), length \(5L\), with a flat bed at sea level. Ice height H(x) is independent of y, symmetric about the divide x=0, and vanishes at x=±L. Use \(\rho_i=917\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(\rho_w=998\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(g=9.82\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), basal friction stress \(S_b=100\,\mathrm{kPa}\). Neglect atmospheric pressure. The integral \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u}\,du=2/3\) may be used. In the dynamical model, incompressible ice flows in the xz plane. Central snowfall adds ice thickness c per year, balanced by melting at the coasts. Near the divide take H≈Hm constant, vx independent of z, vz independent of x and vz=0 at the bed. The historical data and idealizations below are those of the 2013 problem.

3.1. Hydrostatic pressure
Find p(x,z) at height z above the bed.
3.2a. Slab force balance
For x>0, balance horizontal pressure force on a slab of base ΔxΔy against \(S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Write \(S_b=kH\,dH/dx\) and determine k.
3.2b. Ice height profile
Find H(x) and the maximum height Hm. Show the scaling with L.
3.2c. Volume scaling exponent
The island area is A=10L². Find γ in \(V_{ice}\propto A^\gamma\), and derive the volume coefficient.
3.3. Horizontal ice velocity
Use mass conservation in the central region to find vx(x).
3.4. Vertical ice velocity
Using \(\partial_xv_x+\partial_zv_z=0\), find vz(z).
3.5. Particle trajectory
A particle starts at \((x_i,H_m)\). Find its path z(x) in the central approximation.
3.6. Age at the divide
Find the age τ(z) of ice at height z above ground at x=0.
3.7a. Accumulation rates
A 3060 m core has the end of the ice age at depth 1492 m, 11,700 years ago. The ice age began 120,000 years ago at depth 3040 m. Assume Hm=3060 m throughout and constant rates c_ig and c_ia in each period. Find both in m/year.
3.7b. Temperature transition

The supplied graphs relate \(\delta^{18}O=1000(R_{ice}/R_{ref}-1)\) per mille to temperature, with R=[18O]/[16O] and an equatorial-ocean reference. Use the core and calibration plots to estimate the temperature change at the ice-age/interglacial transition.
3.8. Uniform sea level rise
Use Greenland area \(A_G=1.71\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), ocean area \(A_O=3.61\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) and the height profile to find the mean rise after all ice melts.
3.9. Local gravitational tide
Model Greenland ice as a point mass at Earth's surface. Copenhagen is 3500 km along the surface from it. With a global ocean, no rotation, \(M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(R_E=6.38\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), find the sea-level difference between Copenhagen and the point antipodal to Greenland. Work to first order in sea height.

children.text: Integrating \(\partial p/\partial z=-\rho_i g\) with zero surface pressure gives \(p=\rho_i g[H(x)-z]\).

The integrated pressure force per transverse length is \(\rho_i gH^2/2\). Its decrease across the slab gives \(-\rho_i gH H^{\prime}\Delta x\Delta y=S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Thus \(k=-\rho_i g\), including the sign on the positive-x side.
Integrate \(H H^{\prime}=-S_b/(\rho_i g)\) from the coast: \[H(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2S_b}{\rho_i g}(L-|x|)},\qquad H_m=\sqrt{\frac{2S_bL}{\rho_i g}}\propto L^{1/2}.\]
\(V_{ice}=5L\int_{-L}^{L}H(x)dx=(20/3)H_mL^2=(2/3)AH_m\). Since Hm∝L^(1/2), volume scales as L^(5/2) and \(\gamma=5/4\).
Snowfall on a strip from 0 to x supplies volume cx per unit transverse length per year. Outward transport is Hm vx. Thus \(v_x=cx/H_m\).
Dividing the velocities gives \(dz/dx=-z/x\), hence \(xz=H_mx_i\) and \(z=H_mx_i/x\).

For the interglacial period, \(c_{ig}=3060\ln(3060/1568)/11700=0.175\,\mathrm{m/year}\). At the period boundary a particle currently at z=20 m was at \(20(3060/1568)\) m. Equivalently \(c_{ia}=3060\ln(1568/20)/(120000-11700)=0.123\,\mathrm{m/year}\). The two age intervals must be treated separately.
The isotope signal rises from approximately −43.5 to −34.5 per mille. The calibration maps these to roughly −40°C and −28°C, giving a warming of about 12 K. Graph-reading uncertainty is expected.

\(L=\sqrt{A_G/10}=4.14\times10^5\,\mathrm m\), \(H_m\simeq3030\,\mathrm m\), \(V_{ice}=(2/3)A_GH_m=3.45\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Meltwater volume is multiplied by \(\rho_i/\rho_w\). The rise is \(h=(\rho_i/\rho_w)V_{ice}/A_O=8.79\,\mathrm m\).

Let \(M_i=\rho_iV_{ice}\simeq3.17\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}\). At angular distance θ, separation from the ice is \(r=2R_E\sin(\theta/2)\). Constant potential gives \(gh-GM_i/r=\text{constant}\). Thus \[h_{CPH}-h_{opp}=\frac{M_iR_E}{2M_E}\left[\csc\left(\frac{3500\times10^3}{2R_E}\right)-1\right]\simeq4.56\,\mathrm m.\] The ocean is locally higher near the ice. Its loss on melting partially offsets the uniform rise.

solution.text:
The Greenlandic Ice Sheet
3.1. Hydrostatic pressure
Integrating \(\partial p/\partial z=-\rho_i g\) with zero surface pressure gives \(p=\rho_i g[H(x)-z]\).
3.2a. Slab force balance
The integrated pressure force per transverse length is \(\rho_i gH^2/2\). Its decrease across the slab gives \(-\rho_i gH H^{\prime}\Delta x\Delta y=S_b\Delta x\Delta y\). Thus \(k=-\rho_i g\), including the sign on the positive-x side.
3.2b. Ice height profile
Integrate \(H H^{\prime}=-S_b/(\rho_i g)\) from the coast: \[H(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2S_b}{\rho_i g}(L-|x|)},\qquad H_m=\sqrt{\frac{2S_bL}{\rho_i g}}\propto L^{1/2}.\]
3.2c. Volume scaling exponent
\(V_{ice}=5L\int_{-L}^{L}H(x)dx=(20/3)H_mL^2=(2/3)AH_m\). Since Hm∝L^(1/2), volume scales as L^(5/2) and \(\gamma=5/4\).
3.3. Horizontal ice velocity
Snowfall on a strip from 0 to x supplies volume cx per unit transverse length per year. Outward transport is Hm vx. Thus \(v_x=cx/H_m\).
3.4. Vertical ice velocity
\(dv_z/dz=-c/H_m\), and the bed condition fixes \(v_z=-cz/H_m\).
3.5. Particle trajectory
Dividing the velocities gives \(dz/dx=-z/x\), hence \(xz=H_mx_i\) and \(z=H_mx_i/x\).
3.6. Age at the divide
Integrate \(dz/dt=-cz/H_m\) from Hm to z: \[\tau(z)=\frac{H_m}{c}\ln\frac{H_m}{z}.\]
3.7a. Accumulation rates
For the interglacial period, \(c_{ig}=3060\ln(3060/1568)/11700=0.175\,\mathrm{m/year}\). At the period boundary a particle currently at z=20 m was at \(20(3060/1568)\) m. Equivalently \(c_{ia}=3060\ln(1568/20)/(120000-11700)=0.123\,\mathrm{m/year}\). The two age intervals must be treated separately.
3.7b. Temperature transition
The isotope signal rises from approximately −43.5 to −34.5 per mille. The calibration maps these to roughly −40°C and −28°C, giving a warming of about 12 K. Graph-reading uncertainty is expected.
3.8. Uniform sea level rise
\(L=\sqrt{A_G/10}=4.14\times10^5\,\mathrm m\), \(H_m\simeq3030\,\mathrm m\), \(V_{ice}=(2/3)A_GH_m=3.45\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Meltwater volume is multiplied by \(\rho_i/\rho_w\). The rise is \(h=(\rho_i/\rho_w)V_{ice}/A_O=8.79\,\mathrm m\).
3.9. Local gravitational tide
Let \(M_i=\rho_iV_{ice}\simeq3.17\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}\). At angular distance θ, separation from the ice is \(r=2R_E\sin(\theta/2)\). Constant potential gives \(gh-GM_i/r=\text{constant}\). Thus \[h_{CPH}-h_{opp}=\frac{M_iR_E}{2M_E}\left[\csc\left(\frac{3500\times10^3}{2R_E}\right)-1\right]\simeq4.56\,\mathrm m.\] The ocean is locally higher near the ice. Its loss on melting partially offsets the uniform rise.
